title: Overall behavior types are similar across all kinds of simple programs

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Overall behavior types are similar across all kinds of simple programs

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Whatever kind of underlying rules a simple program uses (cellular automata, mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, register machines, symbolic systems), the overall behavior that emerges falls into the same few basic types first seen in elementary cellular automata.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: whatever kind of underlying rules one uses, the behavior that emerges turns out to be remarkably similar to the basic examples that we have already seen in cellular automata.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 3, “The World of Simple Programs”; section “The Search for General Features” (from p. 51), p. 52. Scope: simple programs of all the kinds surveyed in chapter 3

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch03-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing catalogs and new computation can compare all named families over substantial finite rule spaces. They cannot establish the unrestricted all-rules assertion or make the small class taxonomy fully objective.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate bounded samples from each named formalism, extract preregistered trajectory features, and test whether all outputs cluster into the same few behavior classes found in elementary cellular automata. Stable cross-formalism clustering supports the claim; a robust new class refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite enumerations cannot cover whatever kind of underlying rules.

Behavior classes depend on representation and features.

Rare behaviors may be missed.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.65
data existence: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.6

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is comparative and qualitative across the families actually surveyed. Those families have public rule conventions and can be re-simulated, the cellular automata with existing open software and the others from the published diagrams. A shared codebook makes the comparison confirming or refuting. Sampling and fuzzy boundaries are real limits and still leave a weeks-scale analysis that addresses the claim as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Apply one behavior codebook (repetition, nesting, apparent randomness, localized structures) to samples of each program family named in the chapter. The claim is confirmed if each family lands in those classes and refuted if a family produces a stable overall behavior outside the codebook.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Apparent randomness and localized structure are adjacent categories and can be swapped by the statistics chosen.

Large rule spaces are sampled rather than exhausted.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.72
data existence: 0.8
operationalizability: 0.72
data adequacy: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.68
